## Six weeks, zero sensors

Both controllers we have built are **open loop**. The LIPM walker follows a plan
computed before it started moving. The CPG oscillates on a timer. Neither has
ever looked at the robot.

That is why the CPG fell every time, and why the LIPM walker drifts sideways with
nothing to pull it back.

Today the robot finds out about itself. This is the week that makes feedback
possible — and the observation vector we build here is exactly what a learned
policy will consume from Week 8 onward.

In Week 0's loop $y_k = h(x_k)$, this is the week about $h$: the sensors that
**Layer 2** (the robot model) declares, and the first thing a **Layer 4**
controller must do with them — estimate the state it cannot see.

---

## Today, in order {.smaller}

1. **What the simulator knows vs what the robot knows.** The G1 has 12 sensor numbers.
2. **The accelerometer.** It does not measure acceleration. We derive what it
   does measure, and turn it into a tilt angle with `atan2`.
3. **The gyroscope.** It measures a turning rate; adding it up gives an angle
   that drifts, and we derive how fast.
4. **Why not position?** Integrating the accelerometer twice: the error grows
   with *time squared*.
5. **The complementary filter.** One line of code; derived as a low-pass plus a
   high-pass, with a time constant $\tau$ you can read off $\alpha$.
6. **Observable vs privileged.** What a policy may be given, and what only its
   trainer may see.

---

## Colour code for the week {.smaller}

The same colours mean the same things in every equation and every drawing:

| symbol | meaning | colour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$ | **gravity**: $(0, 0, -9.81)\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ in the world, pointing down | <span style="color:#3b7dd8">blue</span> |
| ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}}$ | the body's **own acceleration** (what it is actually doing) | <span style="color:#8e44ad">purple</span> |
| ${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}},\ \theta_{\text{acc}}}$ | the **accelerometer**'s reading, and the angle computed from it | <span style="color:#e8743b">orange</span> |
| ${\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega}}$ | the **gyroscope**'s reading: a turning rate in rad/s | <span style="color:#1a9fb5">cyan</span> |
| ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta}}$ | the **filter's estimate** of an angle (the hat means "estimate") | <span style="color:#2a9d5c">green</span> |
| ${\color{#c0392b}{b,\ e}}$ | a sensor **bias** and the **error** it causes | <span style="color:#c0392b">red</span> |

Uncoloured $\phi, \theta, \psi$ are the **true** roll, pitch and yaw (rotations
about $x$, $y$, $z$ — Week 1). In plots the truth is **dark grey**. The lab's
arrows use the same colours: orange accelerometer, cyan gyro, green filter.

$\Delta t = 0.002$ s is one physics step (500 Hz); $k$ counts steps, so $t = k\,\Delta t$.

---

## The cheating we have been doing {.smaller}

In simulation you can ask the robot anything:

```{python}
try:
    import soc4180
except ImportError:
    %pip install -q "soc4180 @ git+https://github.com/gnoejh/soc4180.git"
    import soc4180

import numpy as np
import mujoco
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

model = soc4180.load_g1()
data = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)

print(f"pelvis position in the world : {np.round(data.qpos[:3], 3)}")
print(f"orientation quaternion       : {np.round(data.qpos[3:7], 3)}")
```

**A real robot knows neither of these.** There is no sensor for "where am I in
the room" and none for absolute attitude. Everything in `qpos[:7]` is
*privileged* information the simulator happens to have.

Build a controller on it and it cannot leave the simulator.

---

## What the G1 actually has {.smaller}

```{python}
for i in range(model.nsensor):
    name = mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_SENSOR, i)
    kind = mujoco.mjtSensor(model.sensor_type[i]).name.replace("mjSENS_", "")
    print(f"  {kind:14s} dim={model.sensor_dim[i]}  {name}")
print(f"\n  total sensordata: {model.nsensordata} numbers")
```

**Two IMUs** (Inertial Measurement Units) — torso and pelvis — each a gyroscope
plus an accelerometer, three axes each. Twelve numbers per timestep, and that is
the entire sensory world of this robot.

No cameras. No joint torque sensors. No foot contact switches. Joint *encoders*
are implicit: a real robot reads its own joint angles, which is why using
`qpos[7:]` is fair while using `qpos[:7]` is not.

## Inside an accelerometer {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def sensor_box(ax, x0, spring_len, title, reading):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0, 0), 1.0, 2.2, fill=False, lw=2, color="0.3"))
    ax.plot([x0 + 0.5, x0 + 0.5], [0.0, 0.0], color="0.3")
    ys = np.linspace(0.0, spring_len, 40)
    ax.plot(x0 + 0.5 + 0.12 * np.sin(ys / spring_len * 8 * np.pi), ys, color="0.45", lw=1.2)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 + 0.3, spring_len), 0.4, 0.35, color="0.55"))
    ax.text(x0 + 0.5, spring_len + 0.175, "m", ha="center", va="center", color="w", fontsize=10)
    ax.text(x0 + 0.5, -0.25, title, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9)
    ax.text(x0 + 0.5, 2.45, reading, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color="#e8743b")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
sensor_box(ax, 0.0, 0.6, "at rest on a table\nspring squashed", "reads $+9.81$ (up)")
sensor_box(ax, 2.6, 0.95, "falling freely\nspring at its natural length", "reads $0$")
sensor_box(ax, 5.2, 0.35, "in a lift accelerating up\nspring squashed more", "reads more than $9.81$")
for x0 in (0.0, 5.2):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 1.25, 0.4), xytext=(x0 + 1.25, 1.2),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#3b7dd8"))
    ax.text(x0 + 1.32, 0.8, "$g$", color="#3b7dd8", fontsize=11)
ax.annotate("", xy=(3.85, 0.4), xytext=(3.85, 1.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#3b7dd8"))
ax.text(3.92, 0.8, "$g$", color="#3b7dd8", fontsize=11)
ax.annotate("", xy=(6.75, 1.9), xytext=(6.75, 1.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#8e44ad"))
ax.text(6.82, 1.5, "$a$", color="#8e44ad", fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 7.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 2.8); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("sketch, not to scale: a proof mass on a spring inside a case bolted to the robot", fontsize=9, color="0.35")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

An accelerometer is a tiny mass $m$ (the **proof mass**) on a spring, inside a
case fixed to the body. The chip measures **how much the spring is squashed** —
nothing else. The next slide turns that into an equation.

---

## What the accelerometer measures, derived {.smaller}

**Step 1 — Newton on the proof mass.** Two forces act on it: the spring's push
$\mathbf{f}_{\text{spring}}$ and gravity $m{\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$. The mass moves with the case, so
its acceleration is the body's, ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}}$:

$$m\,{\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} = \mathbf{f}_{\text{spring}} + m\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$$

**Step 2 — the chip reads only the spring.** Divide the spring force by $m$ and
solve Step 1 for it:

$${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}}} \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{f}_{\text{spring}}}{m} \;=\; {\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$$

This is the **specific force**: every force except gravity, per kilogram.

**Step 3 — in the body's own axes.** The chip is bolted to the body, so it
reports the vector along *its* $x, y, z$. If $R$ is the body's orientation
(body axes → world axes), a world vector is seen in the body as $R^{\mathsf T}$ times it:

$${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}_b}} = R^{\mathsf T}\big({\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}\big)$$

- at rest, ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} = 0$: ${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}}} = -{\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$ = 9.81 m/s² **upward**
- in free fall, ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$: ${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}}} = 0$ — nothing touches the mass

---

## Checking it: at rest and in free fall {.smaller}

```{python}
for _ in range(300):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
gyro, accel = soc4180.read_imu(model, data, "torso")
print(f"at rest     : accel = {np.round(accel, 3)}   |accel| = {np.linalg.norm(accel):.3f}")

falling = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
falling.qpos[2] += 1.0                      # lift it 1 m off the floor and let go
mujoco.mj_forward(model, falling)
mujoco.mj_step(model, falling)
_, accel_ff = soc4180.read_imu(model, falling, "torso")
print(f"in free fall: accel = {np.round(accel_ff, 3)}")
```

Standing still it reads **9.81 along its own $+z$** — up. In free fall it reads
**zero**. Both are exactly Step 2.

That is the whole reason an accelerometer is a *tilt* sensor: at rest the
reading is $-{\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$, so the direction it points **is
"up"**, written in the body's axes. Tilt the body and "up" moves in those axes.

---

## Specific force on a tilted body {.smaller}

A small box carrying one accelerometer, rolled 20° and held still (its
acceleration set to zero and the sensor computed by `mj_inverse`):

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def held_still(roll_deg, pitch_deg, yaw_deg=0.0):
    """Accelerometer reading of a box held still at the given roll, pitch, yaw."""
    q = np.zeros(4)
    mujoco.mju_euler2Quat(q, np.radians([roll_deg, pitch_deg, yaw_deg]), "XYZ")
    m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string("""<mujoco><worldbody><body><freejoint/>
        <geom type="box" size=".05 .03 .02" mass="0.1"/><site name="imu"/></body></worldbody>
        <sensor><accelerometer site="imu"/></sensor></mujoco>""")
    d = mujoco.MjData(m)
    d.qpos[3:7] = q
    d.qacc[:] = 0.0                      # held still: a = 0
    mujoco.mj_inverse(m, d)              # computes the sensors for that acceleration
    return d.sensordata.copy()

f20 = held_still(20, 0)
phi = np.radians(20)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.0))
yb, zb = np.array([np.cos(phi), np.sin(phi)]), np.array([-np.sin(phi), np.cos(phi)])   # body axes in (y, z)
corners = np.array([c1 * 0.3 * yb + c2 * 0.15 * zb for c1, c2 in ((-1, -1), (1, -1), (1, 1), (-1, 1))])
ax.add_patch(plt.Polygon(corners, fill=True, fc="0.92", ec="0.3", lw=1.5, zorder=0))
for v, lab in ((yb, "$y_b$"), (zb, "$z_b$")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=1.3 * v, xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.2, color="0.3"))
    ax.text(*(1.38 * v), lab, fontsize=11, color="0.3")
s = 1.0 / 9.81                            # 1 unit of drawing = 9.81 m/s^2
ax.annotate("", xy=(0, -1.0), xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2.5, color="#3b7dd8"))
ax.text(0.05, -0.95, r"$\mathbf{g}$ (world, down)", color="#3b7dd8", fontsize=10)
ax.annotate("", xy=(0, 1.0), xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2.5, color="#e8743b"))
ax.text(0.06, 1.08, r"$\mathbf{f} = -\mathbf{g}$ (reading)", color="#e8743b", fontsize=10)
py, pz = f20[1] * s * yb, f20[2] * s * zb          # the two components the chip reports
ax.plot(*np.c_[pz, pz + py], ls="--", color="#e8743b", lw=1)
ax.plot(*np.c_[py, py + pz], ls="--", color="#e8743b", lw=1)
ax.plot(*np.c_[[0, 0], py], color="#e8743b", lw=3, alpha=0.5)
ax.plot(*np.c_[[0, 0], pz], color="#e8743b", lw=3, alpha=0.5)
ax.text(*(py + np.array([0.04, -0.12])), f"$f_y$ = {f20[1]:.2f}", color="#e8743b", fontsize=9)
ax.text(*(pz + np.array([-0.55, -0.05])), f"$f_z$ = {f20[2]:.2f}", color="#e8743b", fontsize=9)
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, 0.55], color="0.6", lw=0.8, ls=":")
th = np.linspace(np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2 + phi, 20)
ax.plot(0.5 * np.cos(th), 0.5 * np.sin(th), color="0.2", lw=1)
ax.text(-0.66, 0.28, r"$\phi$ = 20°", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(-1.0, 1.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.45); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("rolled 20° about $x$ ($x$ points out of the page: seen from the front)\n"
             "arrow lengths to scale; the components are the sensor's own numbers", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"accelerometer reading (body axes): f = {np.round(f20, 4)} m/s^2")
```

The vector is the same in the world — 9.81 up. **Only its components in the body
change**: the body's $z$ axis no longer points up, so part of "up" now lies along
the body's $y$.

---

## Tilt from the accelerometer, derived {.smaller}

**Step 1 — assume at rest.** Then ${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}_b}} = -R^{\mathsf T}{\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}} = g\,R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{e}_z$, with $g = 9.81$ and $\mathbf{e}_z = (0,0,1)$ "up".

**Step 2 — write the orientation as three turns**: yaw $\psi$ about $z$, pitch
$\theta$ about $y$, roll $\phi$ about $x$: $\;R = R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\phi)$,
so $R^{\mathsf T} = R_x(\phi)^{\mathsf T} R_y(\theta)^{\mathsf T} R_z(\psi)^{\mathsf T}$.

**Step 3 — yaw drops out.** Turning about the vertical leaves "up" alone:
$R_z(\psi)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{e}_z = \mathbf{e}_z$. **No accelerometer reading can
ever contain yaw.**

**Step 4 — pitch, then roll.** $R_y(\theta)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{e}_z = (-\sin\theta,\ 0,\ \cos\theta)$, and $R_x(\phi)^{\mathsf T}$ of that gives

$${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}_b}} = g\,\big(\,-\sin\theta,\;\; \sin\phi\cos\theta,\;\; \cos\phi\cos\theta\,\big)$$

**Step 5 — divide to cancel what you do not know.**

$$\frac{{\color{#e8743b}{f_y}}}{{\color{#e8743b}{f_z}}} = \tan\phi
\;\Rightarrow\; {\color{#e8743b}{\phi_{\text{acc}}}} = \operatorname{atan2}({\color{#e8743b}{f_y}}, {\color{#e8743b}{f_z}})$$

$$\sqrt{{\color{#e8743b}{f_y}}^2 + {\color{#e8743b}{f_z}}^2} = g\cos\theta
\;\Rightarrow\; {\color{#e8743b}{\theta_{\text{acc}}}} = \operatorname{atan2}\!\big(-{\color{#e8743b}{f_x}},\ \sqrt{{\color{#e8743b}{f_y}}^2 + {\color{#e8743b}{f_z}}^2}\big)$$

- $g$ cancels: only the **direction** of the reading matters, not its size
- `atan2(y, x)`, the angle of the point $(x, y)$, keeps both signs and never divides by zero

---

## Checking the formula {.smaller}

The box from before, held still at known angles; `soc4180.tilt_from_accel` —
Step 5 line for line — reads them back:

```{python}
print(" set: roll  pitch   yaw  |  reading f (m/s^2)            |  atan2 gives: roll   pitch")
for r, p, y in ((20, 0, 0), (0, 30, 0), (20, 30, 0), (20, 30, 45), (20, 30, 170)):
    f = held_still(r, p, y)
    rr, pp = np.degrees(soc4180.tilt_from_accel(f))
    print(f"      {r:4d} {p:6d} {y:5d}  |  {np.array2string(np.round(f, 3), precision=3):30s} |"
          f"  {rr:10.3f} {pp:7.3f}")
```

- the recovered roll and pitch equal the ones set
- the last three rows differ **only in yaw** — and the readings are the same.
  Step 3, measured: gravity is blind to heading.

---

## Gravity is the only compass {.smaller}

On the standing G1, the true gravity direction in the body frame and the tilt
read off the accelerometer:

```{python}
print(f"gravity in the body frame (upright): {np.round(soc4180.gravity_body(data), 4)}")
print(f"roll, pitch from the accelerometer : "
      f"{np.round(np.degrees(soc4180.tilt_from_accel(accel)), 3)} deg")
```

Two things this gives you, and one it does not:

- **roll and pitch** — recoverable (Step 5)
- **yaw** — *not* recoverable (Step 3). A gyroscope can track it for a while,
  but drifts (below); a compass (magnetometer) is unreliable indoors near motors

Locomotion policies therefore observe **gravity in the body frame** rather than
absolute pose. It is the largest piece of attitude a real robot can honestly know.

---

## In simulation the sensors are perfect {.smaller}

```{python}
a = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
b = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
for _ in range(200):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, a); mujoco.mj_step(model, b)
print(f"two identical runs, identical sensordata: {np.array_equal(a.sensordata, b.sensordata)}")
print(f"noise declared in the model: {np.unique(model.sensor_noise)}  (gyro, accel)")
```

The MJCF declares noise magnitudes, but this MuJoCo build applies none — readings
are **exactly** deterministic.

That is convenient and dishonest. A real gyroscope has a slowly wandering bias; a
real accelerometer is noisy and lags. **We will inject those ourselves**, because
an estimator tested on perfect sensors teaches nothing.

---

## Watch the assumption break {.smaller}

Step 1 of the tilt formula assumed ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} = 0$. Walk, and it is not:

```{python}
from soc4180.walking import WalkingController, GaitParams

controller = WalkingController(model, GaitParams(n_steps=8))
sim = controller.initial_data()
imu_site = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_SITE, "imu_in_torso")

log = []
while sim.time < controller.total_time:
    sim.ctrl[:] = controller.control(sim.time)
    mujoco.mj_step(model, sim)
    g, a = soc4180.read_imu(model, sim, "torso")
    # the truth: gravity's direction in the IMU's own frame (site_xmat is IMU -> world)
    down = sim.site_xmat[imu_site].reshape(3, 3).T @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0])
    log.append([sim.time, *g, *a,
                np.arctan2(-down[1], -down[2]),
                np.arctan2(down[0], np.hypot(down[1], down[2]))])

log = np.array(log)
walk = log[log[:, 0] > controller.params.settle_time]
mag = np.linalg.norm(walk[:, 4:7], axis=1)
print(f"walking for {walk[-1, 0] - walk[0, 0]:.1f} s after {controller.params.settle_time:.1f} s of standing")
print(f"|accel| during the walk : {mag.min():.2f} .. {mag.max():.2f} m/s^2   (9.81 if only gravity acted)")
print(f"true roll of the torso  : {np.degrees(walk[:,7]).min():+.2f} .. {np.degrees(walk[:,7]).max():+.2f} deg")
print(f"1 m/s^2 of sideways acceleration reads as {np.degrees(np.arctan2(1, 9.81)):.2f} deg of roll")
```

The truth is taken from the IMU site's own orientation (`site_xmat`) — something
a real robot never has, and exactly what we need to score an estimator.

The last line is Step 2 of the accelerometer derivation at work:
${\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}}} = {\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$, so a sideways
${\color{#8e44ad}{a_y}}$ adds straight into ${\color{#e8743b}{f_y}}$ and the
`atan2` cannot tell it from gravity. Every 1 m/s² of real sideways acceleration
is misread as $\operatorname{atan}(1/9.81)$ = 5.8° of roll — and the reading's
size above strays up to 9.5 m/s² from 9.81.

---

## Seeing the corruption {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
step_times = controller.params.settle_time + controller.params.step_time * np.arange(len(controller.plan) + 1)
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 4.4), sharex=True)
ax0.plot(walk[:, 0], mag, lw=0.8, color="#e8743b", label="|accelerometer|")
ax0.axhline(9.81, color="#3b7dd8", ls="--", lw=1, label="g = 9.81: what a tilt sensor assumes")
ax0.set_ylabel("m/s$^2$"); ax0.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax1.plot(walk[:, 0], np.degrees(walk[:, 7]), lw=1.5, color="0.2", label="true roll")
ax1.plot(walk[:, 0], np.degrees(np.arctan2(walk[:, 5], walk[:, 6])), lw=0.7, color="#e8743b",
         alpha=0.8, label="roll read off the accelerometer")
ax1.set_ylabel("deg"); ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax1.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
for ax in (ax0, ax1):
    for ts in step_times:
        ax.axvline(ts, color="0.6", lw=0.6, ls=":")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The dotted lines are the planned step changes (every
`step_time` = 0.65 s), where one foot lands and the other lifts. The spikes in
the top plot bunch around them, and each lands in the bottom plot as a tilt
that never happened — the body did not roll twenty degrees, the sensor was kicked.

---

## The gyroscope, integrated {.smaller}

A gyroscope reports the body's **turning rate** ${\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega}}$ in
rad/s, about each of its own axes. To get an angle, add it up.

**Step 1 — the model of a real gyro.** The reading is the true rate plus a
**bias** ${\color{#c0392b}{b}}$ — a small constant offset, different on every chip
and wandering with temperature: ${\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}} = \dot\phi_k + {\color{#c0392b}{b}}$.

**Step 2 — integrate, one step at a time** (rectangle rule, like `mj_step`):
$\;{\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\phi_k}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\phi_{k-1}}} + {\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}}\,\Delta t$.

**Step 3 — follow the error** ${\color{#c0392b}{e_k}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\phi_k}} - \phi_k$.
Subtract the truth's own update $\phi_k = \phi_{k-1} + \dot\phi_k\Delta t$:

$${\color{#c0392b}{e_k}} = {\color{#c0392b}{e_{k-1}}} + {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,\Delta t
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
{\color{#c0392b}{e_k}} = {\color{#c0392b}{e_0}} + {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,k\,\Delta t
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
{\color{#c0392b}{e(t)}} = {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t$$

The error grows **in a straight line, for ever**. Nothing in the equation pulls
it back: the gyro has no idea where "up" is, only how fast it is turning.

Read aloud: a bias of 0.01 rad/s is 0.57° every second — **34° after a minute**.
A gyro is right *now* and wrong *later*; the accelerometer was the opposite.

(For roll, $\dot\phi = \omega_x$ exactly only while pitch is zero; on a nearly
upright robot it is close. That approximation, plus the rectangle rule, is the
only error a *perfect* gyro makes here.)

---

## Drift, measured {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
t = walk[:, 0]; gyro_w = walk[:, 1:4]; acc_w = walk[:, 4:7]; roll_true = walk[:, 7]
dt = float(np.mean(np.diff(t)))

def integrate(bias):
    r = np.empty(len(t)); r[0] = roll_true[0]
    for k in range(1, len(t)):
        r[k] = r[k-1] + (gyro_w[k, 0] + bias) * dt
    return r

print(f"a bias of 0.01 rad/s is {np.degrees(0.01):.3f} deg per second, {np.degrees(0.01 * 60):.1f} deg per minute")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.2))
for bias, col in ((0.0, "0.45"), (0.01, "#1a9fb5"), (0.02, "#0b5d6b")):
    err = np.degrees(integrate(bias) - roll_true)
    ax.plot(t - t[0], err, lw=1.4, color=col, label=f"gyro bias {bias} rad/s: measured error")
    print(f"bias {bias:.2f} rad/s: final error {err[-1]:+.2f} deg   predicted b*t = {np.degrees(bias * (t[-1] - t[0])):.2f} deg")
for bias in (0.01, 0.02):
    ax.plot(t - t[0], np.degrees(bias * (t - t[0])), ls="--", color="#c0392b", lw=1)
ax.text(t[-1] - t[0], np.degrees(0.02 * (t[-1] - t[0])), "  $e = b\\,t$", color="#c0392b", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("time since the walk started (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("roll error (deg)")
ax.set_xlim(0, (t[-1] - t[0]) * 1.12)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The grey line is a *perfect* gyro: its wobble (−0.48° at the end) is the
approximation named on the last slide, not the sensor. Each biased line is that
grey line **plus exactly** ${\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t$, the red dashed lines:
at 0.01 rad/s, −0.48 + 2.98 = 2.50°. Drift *is* bias times time, and it only
goes one way.

---

## Neither sensor is enough {.smaller}

```{python}
acc_roll = np.arctan2(acc_w[:, 1], acc_w[:, 2])
acc_err = np.degrees(np.abs(acc_roll - roll_true))
print(f"accelerometer only : mean err {acc_err.mean():5.2f} deg, "
      f"worst {acc_err.max():5.2f} deg, final {acc_err[-1]:5.2f} deg")
for bias in (0.0, 0.01):
    r = integrate(bias)
    print(f"gyroscope only, bias {bias:.3f} rad/s : mean err "
          f"{np.degrees(np.abs(r-roll_true)).mean():5.2f} deg, final err {np.degrees(abs(r[-1]-roll_true[-1])):5.2f} deg")
```

**Complementary failure modes:**

| | error now | error later | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| accelerometer | large (every footfall) | never grows | it always sees gravity, plus ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}}$ |
| gyroscope | tiny | grows as ${\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t$ | it only sees change, never "up" |

A perfect gyro is near-exact — which is precisely why we inject a bias to see the
real problem. The fix is to let each sensor cover the other's weakness.

---

## Why not integrate twice for position? {.smaller}

The accelerometer gives ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}} = R\,{\color{#e8743b}{\mathbf{f}_b}} + {\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$
(Step 3 of the accelerometer derivation, solved for ${\color{#8e44ad}{\mathbf{a}}}$). Integrate once for velocity, twice for position — so why
does no robot do that?

**Step 1 — the error in acceleration.** Suppose the reading carries a bias
${\color{#c0392b}{b}}$ (m/s²). The computed acceleration is ${\color{#8e44ad}{a}} + {\color{#c0392b}{b}}$.

**Step 2 — integrate once:** velocity error ${\color{#c0392b}{e_v(t)}} = \int_0^t {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,ds = {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t$ — the gyro's straight line.

**Step 3 — integrate again:** position error ${\color{#c0392b}{e_p(t)}} = \int_0^t {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,s\,ds = \tfrac12\,{\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t^2$ — a **parabola**.

**Step 4 — the worst bias is gravity.** To subtract ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{g}}}$ you
need $R$, i.e. the tilt. Get the tilt wrong by $\delta$ and a slice of gravity,
${\color{#c0392b}{b}} = g\sin\delta$, is left over as a fake sideways
acceleration.

```{python}
print("position error 1/2 b t^2:         after 1 s   after 10 s   after 60 s")
for name, bias in (("bias 0.01 m/s^2", 0.01),
                   (f"1 deg tilt: b = {9.81 * np.sin(np.radians(1)):.3f} m/s^2", 9.81 * np.sin(np.radians(1)))):
    print(f"  {name:30s}" + "".join(f"{0.5 * bias * T**2:10.3f} m" for T in (1, 10, 60)))
```

The formula's prediction; the next slide measures it on the robot.

---

## Double integration, measured {.smaller}

The G1 standing still for 20 s — its true position does not change — and the
accelerometer integrated twice, three ways:

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
still = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
q_err, tilt_err = np.zeros(4), np.zeros(9)
mujoco.mju_euler2Quat(q_err, np.radians([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), "XYZ")
mujoco.mju_quat2Mat(tilt_err, q_err); tilt_err = tilt_err.reshape(3, 3)   # a 1-degree pitch mistake
g_world = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -9.81])
cases = {"exact tilt, no bias": (np.eye(3), 0.0),
         "exact tilt, bias 0.01 m/s^2": (np.eye(3), 0.01),
         "tilt wrong by 1 deg": (tilt_err, 0.0)}
vel = {k: np.zeros(3) for k in cases}; pos = {k: np.zeros(3) for k in cases}
trace = {k: [] for k in cases}; times = []
mujoco.mj_forward(model, still); start = still.site_xpos[imu_site].copy()
for _ in range(int(20.0 / model.opt.timestep)):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, still)
    _, f_b = soc4180.read_imu(model, still, "torso")
    R = still.site_xmat[imu_site].reshape(3, 3)
    for k, (err_R, bias) in cases.items():
        a_world = err_R @ R @ (f_b + np.array([bias, 0.0, 0.0])) + g_world
        vel[k] += a_world * model.opt.timestep
        pos[k] += vel[k] * model.opt.timestep
        trace[k].append(np.linalg.norm(pos[k][:2]))
    times.append(still.time)
times = np.array(times)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.2))
for (k, tr), col in zip(trace.items(), ("0.2", "#e8743b", "#c0392b")):
    ax.loglog(times, np.maximum(tr, 1e-9), lw=1.6, color=col, label=f"measured: {k}")
for bias in (0.01, 9.81 * np.sin(np.radians(1))):
    ax.loglog(times, 0.5 * bias * times**2, ls="--", lw=1, color="#3b7dd8")
ax.text(0.004, 20, r"blue dashed: the formula $\frac{1}{2}\,b\,t^2$", color="#3b7dd8", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("integrated horizontal\nposition (m)")
ax.set_ylim(1e-8, 1e3); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for k, tr in trace.items():
    print(f"{k:28s}: {tr[int(1/model.opt.timestep)-1]:9.4f} m at 1 s, "
          f"{tr[int(10/model.opt.timestep)-1]:8.3f} m at 10 s, {tr[-1]:8.4f} m at 20 s")
print(f"{'true horizontal sway of the IMU':28s}: {np.linalg.norm((still.site_xpos[imu_site] - start)[:2]):41.4f} m at 20 s")
```

Log–log axes: a straight line of **slope 2** is $t^2$. With a perfect sensor and
the exact tilt (dark grey) the integral tracks the body's real sway — about half
a millimetre, the last printed line. Add a 0.01 m/s² bias or a 1° tilt mistake
and the result sits on the parabola, exactly as predicted: 2 m and 34 m after 20 s
of standing still. **Position needs a sensor that sees the
world** (cameras, GPS, contact with known ground) — the G1 has none, which is why
position is privileged.

---

## Blend them: the complementary filter {.smaller}

Trust the gyroscope over short intervals; let gravity correct it slowly. Three
steps every tick:

**Step 1 — predict** with the gyro: $\;{\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta^{-}_k}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta_{k-1}}} + {\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}}\,\Delta t$

**Step 2 — measure** with the accelerometer: $\;{\color{#e8743b}{\theta_{\text{acc},k}}} = \operatorname{atan2}(\dots)$ from the tilt slide

**Step 3 — blend**, with one number $\alpha$ between 0 and 1:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta_k}} = \alpha\,\big({\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta_{k-1}}} + {\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}}\,\Delta t\big) \;+\; (1-\alpha)\,{\color{#e8743b}{\theta_{\text{acc},k}}}$$

- $\alpha = 1$: pure gyro (drifts). $\alpha = 0$: pure accelerometer (kicked by every step)
- $\alpha = 0.995$: each tick, move 0.5 % of the way from the gyro's prediction
  toward the accelerometer's angle. A footfall spike lasting a few ticks barely
  moves it; a bias that pushes the same way for seconds is pulled back

```{python}
def run_filter(alpha, bias=0.01):
    f = soc4180.ComplementaryFilter(dt=dt, alpha=alpha, roll=roll_true[0])
    out = []
    for k in range(len(t)):
        g = gyro_w[k].copy(); g[0] += bias          # a realistically biased gyro
        out.append(f.update(g, acc_w[k])[0])
    return np.array(out)

for alpha in (0.90, 0.98, 0.995, 1.0):
    est = run_filter(alpha)
    label = "1.0 (gyro only)" if alpha == 1.0 else f"{alpha}"
    print(f"  alpha = {label:<16} mean err {np.degrees(np.abs(est-roll_true)).mean():5.2f} deg,"
          f"  final err {np.degrees(abs(est[-1]-roll_true[-1])):5.2f} deg")
```

---

## Reading the table {.smaller}

```{python}
est995 = run_filter(0.995); gyro_only = run_filter(1.0)
print(f"alpha 0.995 : mean {np.degrees(np.abs(est995 - roll_true)).mean():.2f}  final {np.degrees(abs(est995[-1] - roll_true[-1])):.2f} deg")
print(f"alpha 1.0   : mean {np.degrees(np.abs(gyro_only - roll_true)).mean():.2f}  final {np.degrees(abs(gyro_only[-1] - roll_true[-1])):.2f} deg")
```

- $\alpha = 0.90$ and $0.98$ trust the accelerometer too much: the footfalls leak
  straight through, and the error is several degrees.
- $\alpha = 0.995$ beats the gyro alone on the **final** error.
- Compare the *mean* and *final* columns for $\alpha = 1$: the pure gyro starts
  exact and walks away as $b\,t$, so over a 5-second walk its **mean** hides a
  **final** error that keeps growing. Drift only grows — which is why mean error
  is the wrong way to judge an estimator you intend to run for an hour.

Why does $\alpha = 0.995$ stop the drift? The next three slides answer it.

---

## The filter as two filters, derived {.smaller}

Write $z^{-1}$ for "one step ago": $z^{-1}\Theta$ means $\theta_{k-1}$. (This
is the **$z$-transform**; here it is just shorthand for a delay.)

**Step 1 — the update, rearranged:** ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta_k}} - \alpha\,{\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\theta_{k-1}}} = \alpha\,\Delta t\,{\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}} + (1-\alpha)\,{\color{#e8743b}{\theta_{\text{acc},k}}}$

**Step 2 — in shorthand, and solve for the estimate:**

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\Theta}} = \underbrace{\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}}_{L(z)}\;{\color{#e8743b}{\Theta_{\text{acc}}}}
\;+\; \frac{\alpha\,\Delta t}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}\;{\color{#1a9fb5}{\Omega}}$$

**Step 3 — say what the gyro is measuring.** A perfect gyro reads the change in
the true angle: ${\color{#1a9fb5}{\omega_k}}\,\Delta t = \theta_k - \theta_{k-1}$, i.e. ${\color{#1a9fb5}{\Omega}}\,\Delta t = (1 - z^{-1})\,\Theta$. Substitute:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\Theta}} = L(z)\,{\color{#e8743b}{\Theta_{\text{acc}}}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\alpha\,(1-z^{-1})}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}}_{H(z)}\;\Theta$$

---

## A low-pass plus a high-pass {.smaller}

From the last slide: ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\hat\Theta}} = L(z)\,{\color{#e8743b}{\Theta_{\text{acc}}}} + H(z)\,\Theta$, with
$L = \dfrac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}$ and $H = \dfrac{\alpha\,(1-z^{-1})}{1-\alpha z^{-1}}$.

**Step 4 — add the two filters:** $L + H = \dfrac{1-\alpha + \alpha - \alpha z^{-1}}{1-\alpha z^{-1}} = 1$. **They sum to one.**

- $L$ at a constant signal ($z = 1$): gain $1$. At a fast one: gain near $0$. A **low-pass**.
- $H = 1 - L$: passes fast changes, blocks constants. A **high-pass**.
- So the estimate is the **slow part of the accelerometer's angle plus the fast
  part of the gyro's**. If both sensors were perfect you would get $\theta$ back exactly.

---

## The time constant $\tau$, derived {.smaller}

**Step 1 — kick the filter once.** Feed $L$ a single accelerometer reading of 1
at $k = 0$ and zeros after. The update gives $1-\alpha$, then $(1-\alpha)\alpha$,
then $(1-\alpha)\alpha^2$ … — the memory decays as $\alpha^k$.

**Step 2 — write it as an exponential in time.** $\alpha^k = e^{k\ln\alpha}$, and $k = t/\Delta t$:

$$\alpha^k = e^{\,t\,\ln\alpha/\Delta t} = e^{-t/\tau}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\;\tau = -\frac{\Delta t}{\ln\alpha}\;} \;\approx\; \frac{\Delta t}{1-\alpha}\ \text{ for } \alpha \text{ near } 1$$

($\ln\alpha < 0$, so $\tau > 0$; the approximation is $\ln\alpha \approx \alpha - 1$.)

**Step 3 — the crossover frequency** is $f_c = 1/(2\pi\tau)$: slower than $f_c$ the
accelerometer wins, faster the gyro wins.

**Step 4 — what happens to the bias.** Standing still, the accelerometer is
right and the gyro reads ${\color{#c0392b}{b}}$. The error settles where the
update stops changing it: ${\color{#c0392b}{e}} = \alpha({\color{#c0392b}{e}} + {\color{#c0392b}{b}}\Delta t)$, so

$${\color{#c0392b}{e_\infty}} = \frac{\alpha\,\Delta t}{1-\alpha}\,{\color{#c0392b}{b}} \;\approx\; \tau\,{\color{#c0392b}{b}}$$

**Bounded**, instead of ${\color{#c0392b}{b}}\,t$. Trust the gyro for $\tau$
seconds and you inherit $\tau$ seconds' worth of its bias — never more.

---

## $\tau$ in numbers {.smaller}

```{python}
print(f"dt = {dt:.4f} s")
print(" alpha    tau (s)   f_c (Hz)   bias error tau*b at b = 0.01 rad/s")
for alpha in (0.98, 0.995, 0.998, 0.999):
    tau = -dt / np.log(alpha)
    print(f" {alpha:<7} {tau:8.3f}  {1 / (2 * np.pi * tau):9.3f}   "
          f"{np.degrees(alpha * dt / (1 - alpha) * 0.01):6.3f} deg")

# Step 4 measured: the robot stands still for 10 s with a biased gyro
still = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
cf = soc4180.ComplementaryFilter(dt=model.opt.timestep, alpha=0.995)
for _ in range(int(10.0 / model.opt.timestep)):
    mujoco.mj_step(model, still)
    g, a = soc4180.read_imu(model, still, "torso")
    cf.update(g + np.array([0.01, 0.0, 0.0]), a)
down = still.site_xmat[imu_site].reshape(3, 3).T @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0])
print(f"\nstanding 10 s, bias 0.01 rad/s, alpha 0.995: filter error "
      f"{np.degrees(cf.roll - np.arctan2(-down[1], -down[2])):.3f} deg "
      f"(gyro alone would be {np.degrees(0.01 * 10):.1f} deg)")
```

Read the second row aloud: at $\alpha = 0.995$ the filter remembers the gyro for
about 0.4 s, hands over to the accelerometer below about 0.4 Hz, and a
0.01 rad/s bias costs a fixed quarter of a degree instead of a growing error.

---

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.0))
```

The one-line update and this diagram are the same thing: Step 4 of the
derivation showed that $L$ and $H$ fall out of it by algebra. The code never

---

## The filter in frequency {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
freqs = np.logspace(-2, 2, 400)
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 4.6), sharex=True)
for alpha, ls in ((0.98, ":"), (0.995, "-"), (0.999, "--")):
    zinv = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * freqs * dt)
    L = (1 - alpha) / (1 - alpha * zinv)
    tau = -dt / np.log(alpha)
    ax0.semilogx(freqs, np.abs(L), lw=2, ls=ls, color="#e8743b", label=fr"$|L|$, $\alpha$ = {alpha} ($\tau$ = {tau:.2f} s)")
    ax0.semilogx(freqs, np.abs(1 - L), lw=1.2, ls=ls, color="#1a9fb5")
fc = 1 / (2 * np.pi * (-dt / np.log(0.995)))
ax0.axvline(fc, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
ax0.text(fc * 1.1, 0.03, f"$f_c$ = {fc:.2f} Hz\n($\\alpha$ = 0.995)", fontsize=8, color="0.3")
ax0.text(0.012, 0.88, "orange: accelerometer path $|L|$", fontsize=8, color="#e8743b")
ax0.text(12, 0.88, "cyan: gyro path $|H|$", fontsize=8, color="#1a9fb5")
ax0.set_ylabel("gain"); ax0.set_ylim(0, 1.05); ax0.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="center right"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)

err = acc_roll - roll_true                       # what the accelerometer gets wrong while walking
spec_f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(err), dt)
spec = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(err - err.mean())); spec /= spec.max()
ax1.semilogx(spec_f[1:], spec[1:], color="#e8743b", lw=1)
stride_hz = 1 / (2 * controller.params.step_time)
ax1.axvline(stride_hz, color="0.4", lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax1.text(stride_hz * 1.08, 0.85, f"stride {stride_hz:.2f} Hz", fontsize=8, color="0.3")
ax1.axvline(fc, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
ax1.text(0.012, 0.55, "gyro bias $b$: a constant,\nsits at 0 Hz, off the left edge", fontsize=8, color="#c0392b")
ax1.set_ylabel("accelerometer's\nerror (relative)"); ax1.set_xlabel("frequency (Hz)"); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax1.set_xlim(0.01, 100)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
peak = spec_f[1:][np.argmax(spec[1:])]
print(f"accelerometer error: largest component at {peak:.2f} Hz; stride frequency {stride_hz:.2f} Hz")
for alpha in (0.995, 0.998):
    gain = lambda fr: abs((1 - alpha) / (1 - alpha * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * fr * dt)))
    print(f"alpha {alpha}: |L| = {gain(stride_hz):.3f} at the stride, {gain(peak):.3f} at {peak:.2f} Hz")
```

**Top:** what each path lets through. **Bottom:** where the accelerometer's
walking error lives, measured by Fourier transform of the error two plots back.
One stride is two steps (left, right), so the stride frequency is
$1/(2 \times 0.65\ \text{s})$; the error has peaks there and at its odd
multiples, the tallest at three times it (2.31 Hz).

---

## Reading the frequency picture {.smaller}

The filter works because the two sensors' errors sit in **different frequency
bands**: the gyro's bias at 0 Hz (removed by the high-pass), the footfalls from
0.77 Hz up (cut by the low-pass). But read the printout: at $\alpha = 0.995$
almost half of the stride component still gets through — the crossover at
0.40 Hz is too close to 0.77 Hz. Moving to $\alpha = 0.998$ ($f_c$ = 0.16 Hz)
cuts it harder, at the price of a larger $\tau b$:

| $\alpha$ | $f_c$ | stride (0.77 Hz) let through | 2.31 Hz let through | bias error $\tau b$ at 0.01 rad/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.995 | 0.40 Hz | 46 % | 17 % | 0.23° |
| 0.998 | 0.16 Hz | 20 % | 7 % | 0.57° |

Every number is printed two or three slides back. Lowering $f_c$ buys less footfall
and pays more bias: that is the whole trade, and the next slide finds its balance.

---

## What $\alpha$ really sets {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
alphas = 1 - np.logspace(-3.3, -1, 25)
mean_err, final_err = [], []
for alpha in alphas:
    est = run_filter(alpha)
    mean_err.append(np.degrees(np.abs(est - roll_true)).mean())
    final_err.append(np.degrees(abs(est[-1] - roll_true[-1])))
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.3))
ax1.semilogx(1 - alphas, mean_err, "o-", ms=4, lw=1.5, color="#2a9d5c", label="mean error")
ax1.semilogx(1 - alphas, final_err, "s-", ms=4, lw=1.5, color="#c0392b", label="final error (drift)")
ax1.set_xlabel(r"$1 - \alpha$   (left: trust the gyro longer;  right: trust gravity sooner)")
ax1.set_ylabel("roll error (deg)"); ax1.legend(fontsize=8)
ax1.set_title("biased gyro (0.01 rad/s), walking: both errors against alpha", fontsize=10); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
best_mean, best_final = alphas[np.argmin(mean_err)], alphas[np.argmin(final_err)]
print(f"mean error is smallest at alpha = {best_mean:.4f} (tau = {-dt / np.log(best_mean):.2f} s), "
      f"final error at alpha = {best_final:.4f} (tau = {-dt / np.log(best_final):.2f} s)")
```

Go **left** (larger $\tau$) and the bias error $\tau{\color{#c0392b}{b}}$ grows;
go **right** (smaller $\tau$) and more of the footfall band passes $L$. The minimum
is where those two costs balance, so where it sits depends on how bad each
sensor is: by the same two costs, a worse bias should push it right and a
rougher gait left (exercise 2 lets you test that). **$\alpha$ is not
a constant, it is a claim about your sensors.**

```{python}
ax.plot(t, np.degrees(integrate(0.01)), lw=1.2, ls="--", color="#1a9fb5", label="gyro only (bias 0.01 rad/s)")
ax.plot(t, np.degrees(run_filter(0.995)), lw=1.4, color="#2a9d5c", label="complementary, $\\alpha$=0.995")

ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The cyan dashed line walks away ($b\,t$). The orange line is jagged (the footfall
band). The green line follows the grey truth: the slow part of the orange plus
the fast part of the cyan.

## Observable and privileged, defined {.smaller}

The simulator holds the **full state** $s$: every `qpos`, every `qvel`, every
contact force, the friction, the terrain. A robot's sensors see a function of it:

$$o = h(s) + \text{noise}$$

- $o$ — the **observation**: what the sensors report (here, IMU numbers and
  encoders). Week 0 wrote the same thing as $y_k = h(x_k)$; from Week 7 on it is $o$ and $s$
- $h$ — the **sensor model**: which parts of $s$ reach a sensor, and in which frame
- **observable**: anything you can compute from $o$ (possibly through a filter,
  like today's tilt)
- **privileged**: anything in $s$ that no function of $o$ recovers — world
  position, heading, height above the floor, contact forces on this robot

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.3))
```

## Designing an observation {.smaller}

This is the week's real product. What may a policy be given?

| Quantity | Real robot? | Use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joint angles `qpos[7:]` | encoders | **yes** |
| Joint velocities `qvel[6:]` | differentiated encoders | **yes** |
| Gravity in body frame | IMU + filter (today) | **yes** |
| Angular velocity | gyroscope | **yes** |
| Previous action | it commanded it | **yes** |
| Body height `qpos[2]` | no sensor | no |
| World position `qpos[:2]` | no sensor; double integration diverges | no |
| Yaw (heading) | gravity is blind to it; the gyro drifts | no |
| Foot contact forces | not on this robot | no |

```{python}
obs = np.concatenate([
    soc4180.gravity_body(sim),                       # 3
    soc4180.read_imu(model, sim, "torso")[0],        # 3 angular velocity
    sim.qpos[7:],                                    # 29 joint angles
    sim.qvel[6:],                                    # 29 joint velocities
])
print(f"observation vector: {obs.shape[0]} numbers, every one measurable on hardware")
```

One honest caveat: this cell takes gravity from `gravity_body`, the simulator's
exact answer, standing in for what today's filter would estimate. Week 7's
environment does the same. On hardware that entry comes from a filter, with
the errors we just measured.

## Privileged information {.smaller}

Some quantities are unavailable at deployment but *known* during training — body
height, contact forces, the terrain, the friction coefficient.

Throwing them away entirely is wasteful. Reinforcement learning (Week 8) trains
two networks, and only one of them goes onto the robot:

- the **actor** (the policy) chooses actions, and runs on the robot — so it sees
  only $o$, what a real robot can measure
- the **critic** (the value function) only scores states *during training* and
  is discarded afterwards — so it may see all of $s$

This is **asymmetric actor-critic**: asymmetric because the two networks get
different inputs (the drawing two slides back). The critic's better view makes
its scores more accurate, which makes the actor learn faster; the actor stays
deployable. You will meet it again in Week 10, where production G1 training
does exactly this.

The discipline starts today: *what does the robot know, and how does it know it?*

## Exercises {.smaller}

1. **Noise, properly.** Add Gaussian noise to the accelerometer at the magnitude
   the MJCF declares (0.01). How much does the accelerometer-only estimate
   degrade, and how much does the filter?
2. **Sweep $\alpha$.** Plot mean and final error against $\alpha$ from 0.9 to
   1.0. Where is the optimum, and how sharp is it?
3. **Latency.** Delay the IMU by 20 ms before filtering. Which estimator suffers
   most, and does a different $\alpha$ compensate?
4. **The second IMU.** The pelvis IMU has been ignored all lecture. Does
   averaging both improve the estimate? Explain the result either way.
5. **Yaw.** Try to estimate yaw from these sensors. Show where it fails, and say
   what hardware would fix it.
6. **Close the loop.** Feed the estimated roll back into the Week 4 walker as a
   small lateral correction. Does it reduce the sideways drift?
7. **Check $\tau b$.** Stand the robot still with gyro biases of 0.005, 0.01 and
   0.02 rad/s and $\alpha$ = 0.99, 0.995, 0.998. Does the settled error match
   $\alpha\Delta t\,b/(1-\alpha)$ in every case?
